choices.text: Because the fee depends on how many apps you publish

choices.text: Because this course is about Apple first
choices.why: The course treats both platforms evenly.

prompt: According to Apple, which guideline accounts for over 40% of unresolved review issues?

choices.text: 5.1, Privacy
choices.why: Privacy is on the list, but not the 40%.

choices.text: 3.1, Payments inside the app
choices.why: Not the one Apple names.

choices.text: 4.1, Copycats and impersonation
choices.why: Copycats are rejected, but they are not the largest share.

choices.text: 2.1, App Completeness
choices.why: Right: crashes, placeholder content, incomplete information.

prompt: The planner asks for an account on its first screen. What must its App Store submission include?

choices.text: The source code, so the reviewer can skip the login
choices.why: Reviewers use the app, not its source.

choices.text: A working demo account, with the server up
choices.why: Right. Guideline 2.1 asks for demo account info, and to turn the back-end on; without one the reviewer sees nothing past the login.

choices.text: A video of somebody signing in
choices.why: A video does not let the reviewer use the rest of the app.

choices.text: Nothing extra: reviewers create their own accounts
choices.why: Apple asks for a demo account precisely because they do not.

prompt: Which of these appear in Apple's list of common review issues? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: broken links
choices.why: Every link must work, including support and privacy policy.

choices.text: placeholder content
choices.why: Sample text and empty screens are rejected.

choices.text: an app written in Kotlin
choices.why: The language is not a review issue, and Kotlin is Android's.

choices.text: crashes and bugs
choices.why: Test on devices with the latest software first.

choices.text: a build number above 100
choices.why: Build numbers only have to grow.

prompt: What does Google Play's pre-launch report do?

choices.text: Sends the build to a human reviewer first
choices.why: It runs the build on devices; that is the point of it.

choices.text: Runs it on many devices and reports problems
choices.why: Right: stability, compatibility, performance, accessibility and security, all five, on the closed and open tracks.

choices.text: Publishes the app to 1% of users
choices.why: That would be a staged release, not a report.

choices.text: Translates the store listing into every language
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson's source says so.

prompt: An app's privacy information says it collects no location, and the app asks for location to suggest study places. What happens in review, and why?

choices.text: Nothing: the declaration is only read by users
choices.why: Review compares declarations with what the app does.

choices.text: It passes, because asking is not collecting
choices.why: An app that asks for location to use it is collecting it.

choices.text: Apple removes the location permission automatically
choices.why: Review sends the app back; it does not edit it.

choices.text: Sent back: the two statements contradict
choices.why: Right. Review compares the declaration with the app, and both cannot be true.

prompt: Up to how many external testers can a TestFlight beta have, per Apple's page?
Why can't the planner's beta be sent to a friend's iPhone as a file, as it can to an Android phone?

choices.text: An iPhone installs only what Apple signed
choices.why: Right. That is why TestFlight exists.

choices.text: Because iPhone apps are too large to send by email
choices.why: Size is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Because iOS has no file manager
choices.why: It has one; installing from a file is what it does not allow.

choices.text: Because the friend needs a developer account to open it
choices.why: A TestFlight tester needs no developer account.

prompt: What must happen before external TestFlight testers get the planner's first build?

choices.text: Nothing: TestFlight skips review
choices.why: Internal testing has no review step named; external testing does.

choices.text: The app must be live on the App Store
choices.why: TestFlight is for before release.

choices.text: App Review approves it
choices.why: Right. External testers only get a build App Review approved; significant updates go back to review too.

choices.text: Each tester pays the developer membership
choices.why: Testers pay nothing.

prompt: A tester writes "the week's total is wrong". What does the lesson say makes that report useful?

choices.text: The build number of the build they ran
choices.why: Right. Every build carries its own, and only it says exactly which code ran.

choices.text: The tester's phone model
choices.why: Worth having, but the lesson names something else first.

choices.text: The version name, such as 1.10.0
choices.why: Two builds can share a name, as 42 and 43 did.

choices.text: A screenshot of the total
choices.why: Useful, but it does not say which code produced it.

prompt: On Android, which number does the system compare to prevent a downgrade?

choices.text: CFBundleVersion
choices.why: That is iOS's build number.

choices.text: versionName
choices.why: That is the one users read; Android does not compare it.

choices.text: versionCode
choices.why: Right. An APK with a lower versionCode than the installed one is refused.

choices.text: The date of the build
choices.why: Dates are not compared.

prompt: As text, "1.10.0" sorts before "1.9.2", because the character 1 comes before ___.
Against a published 1.9.2 build 41, version.ts refuses 1.10.0 build 41. Why?

choices.text: Because 1.10.0 is older than 1.9.2
choices.why: As versions it is newer; only as text does it look older.

choices.text: Its build number, 41, is not higher than the published 41
choices.why: Right. 41 is used, and a used versionCode can never be uploaded again.

choices.text: Because the name has more than two dots
choices.why: 1.10.0 has two dots, which is the required three-part form.

choices.text: Because a minor version may not jump from 9 to 10
choices.why: It can; the numbers are compared as numbers.

prompt: A team ships 1.9.2 again with build 43, after fixing a crash in build 41. Does version.ts accept it, and what is this called?

choices.text: Refused, because the name did not grow
choices.why: The name may stay the same; it must only not go back.

choices.text: Refused, because 43 skips 42
choices.why: Build numbers must grow, not grow by one.

choices.text: Accepted, but only on Android
choices.why: The check is the same for both platforms' numbers.

choices.text: Accepted, as a rebuild
choices.why: Right. The name only must not go back, and the build grew: that is the last line of the output.

prompt: Match each key to its platform and job.
In Apple's phased release, what percentage of users with automatic updates get the version on day 3?
What happens during a pause in Apple's phased release?

choices.text: Nobody can download it, even by hand
choices.why: Anyone can download it by hand at any time; phases govern automatic updates.

choices.text: The version is removed from phones that installed it
choices.why: Nothing is uninstalled from anyone's phone.

choices.text: No new users get it; those who have it keep it
choices.why: Right. Pausing stops the spreading, nothing is removed, and the schedule resumes where it left off.

choices.text: The schedule restarts from day 1 when resumed
choices.why: It picks up on the day it left off.

prompt: A version with a bad bug has reached 20% of users. What can the team do for the phones that already have it?

choices.text: Ship a newer, fixed build
choices.why: Right. A bad release is only ever fixed forwards; the phased release kept the 20% from being 100%.

choices.text: Re-upload the previous build with its old number
choices.why: A used build number cannot be reused.

choices.text: Roll those phones back to the previous build
choices.why: There is no rolling a phone back.

choices.text: Ask the store to uninstall it remotely
choices.why: Neither store uninstalls your version from users' phones.
